snippet.title: The Plague That Accidentally Built the Modern World
snippet.description:
The Black Death killed between a third and half of Europe's population. It was one of the greatest catastrophes in human history. And it accidentally dismantled a social system that had seemed permanent for centuries.

This is Episode 2 of World History — The Untold Story.


0:20 A ship arrives in Sicily, October 1347
0:44 The World Before — Feudalism and the rigid order
1:26 The Collapse of Labor — When workers became scarce
1:54 The New Power — Peasants at the crossroads
2:19 The Nobles Fight Back — The Statute of Labourers, 1351
3:11 The Slow Transformation — Wages, markets, and mobility
4:16 An Unexpected Ripple — Watermills, windmills, and the printing press
5:10 The Darker Thread — Fear, blame, and cruelty
5:53 Closing — How permanent are the systems we live inside today?

Feudalism did not collapse in a single dramatic year. It eroded slowly, estate by estate, negotiation by negotiation — pushed along by a labor market that had been violently, permanently rebalanced by a disease no one could stop.

This is the second chapter in our series on the untold stories that shaped world history.

snippet.title: Life After Chernobyl and Fukushima | Full Documentary
snippet.description:
Thirty years after Chernobyl and five years after Fukushima, millions of people continue to live on lands quietly marked by radioactive contamination.

This documentary enters the “grey zones” of Belarus, Norway, and Japan, where the consequences of nuclear disaster are not only historical, but part of everyday life. After Chernobyl, the scientific program Ethos was launched with support from France and the European Union to work directly with communities in contaminated territories, helping residents identify daily risks, adapt their behaviors, and continue living in affected areas.

In central Norway, heavy fallout from Chernobyl deeply disrupted the lives of the Sami people, whose traditional reindeer herding practices were severely impacted by radioactivity. Decades later, Japan faced similar questions after Fukushima, where Ethos-inspired meetings brought together people from Belarus, Norway, and Japan to share experiences, fears, knowledge, and survival strategies.

Through rare personal testimony and unique encounters across three countries, the film asks urgent human questions: What does it mean to live in a contaminated territory? What risks remain invisible? And how do communities rebuild daily life in the long shadow of nuclear disaster?

snippet.title: Is Inflation or Deflation Worse for You?
snippet.description:
Inflation eats away at your money’s value. Deflation freezes the economy. In this short, we compare these two powerful economic forces and explain why both can be dangerous if they spiral out of control.

You’ll learn:

The difference between inflation and deflation

How inflation reduces purchasing power

Why deflation can stall growth and investment

Why central banks aim for stable, low inflation

Healthy economies walk a fine line—too much inflation or deflation can harm jobs, wages, and savings. This is why policymakers target a small, steady inflation rate to keep markets stable and predictable.

Related topics in this video: inflation meaning, deflation meaning, hyperinflation, deflationary spiral, central bank targets, price stability, economic cycles, purchasing power, cost of living, interest rate policy.

snippet.title: 12 Things Poor People Think Are Assets (But Aren’t)
snippet.description:
12 Things Poor People Think Are Assets (But Aren’t)

Most people believe they are building wealth. They buy a house, a car, expensive clothes, insurance policies, and other things that feel like ownership. But what if many of the things we believe are assets are actually quietly draining our money?

In this video, we break down 12 things poor and middle-class people often think are assets — but financially behave like liabilities.

 From cars and homes to collectibles, jewelry, and even cash, these items are widely marketed as symbols of wealth and financial progress. 

Yet when you examine the numbers, many of them lose value, require constant spending, or fail to generate any income at all.

You’ll learn the difference between true assets and consumption items, and why understanding this distinction can completely change how you think about money.

This video explores historical trends, financial behavior, and economic systems that shape how everyday people build—or lose—wealth over time.

If you want to understand how wealth is really built and why so many people unknowingly fall into financial traps, this analysis will change the way you see money forever.

snippet.title: Fall Asleep to History: The Mississippi Bubble & France’s Financial Disaster
snippet.description:
Tonight, we drift back to 18th-century France to explore one of history’s most fascinating financial disasters: The Mississippi Bubble of 1720. In this relaxing sleep story, we follow the incredible rise and fall of John Law, a Scottish gambler turned economic theorist who convinced a desperate kingdom to bet its future on paper money and the promise of Louisiana.

Discover how the frenzy of speculation consumed Paris, created the first "millionaires," and eventually led to a catastrophic crash that changed financial history forever. Designed to help you relax and disconnect, this calm narration guides you through the complexities of the Banque Royale, the Company of the West, and the psychology of the bubble, allowing the details of history to lull you into a deep, peaceful sleep.

snippet.title: How a Teenage Boy Fooled the Nazis and Lived - The incredible story of film producer Gene Gutowski
snippet.description:
Film producer Gene Gutowski (Repulsion, Cul-de-Sac, The Pianist) was fourteen years old when first the Soviets then the Nazis invaded his hometown of Lwow, Poland. With a combination of chutzpah, cunning and an unflinching will to live, he survived the war flirting with danger as a teenage boy hiding in plain site. 

Witnessing first-hand the unspeakable horrors of the Nazi occupation, frequently cheating death and losing his entire family, Gutowski's journey is ultimately one of hope. As recounted with humour and pathos to his son, filmmaker Adam Bardach, his remarkable story represents a thumb of the nose at darkness and totalitarianism.

-------

snippet.title: Why LA will never get a Mayor Zohran Mamdani
snippet.description:
With the election of Zohran Mamdani in New York City, big-city mayors have once again become a focal point of national politics. 

Now, in Los Angeles, the mayoral race in November is heating up with Councilmember Nithya Raman edging out reality TV star Spencer Pratt to secure her candidacy against incumbent Mayor Karen Bass. And Raman, a Democratic Socialist like Mamdani, is zeroing in on housing and affordability as defining issues of local politics.

But beneath the promises to take on hot-button issues that plague Angelenos, a persistent question remains: Why can’t the LA mayor get anything done?

Part of the answer takes us back to the creation of the LA city charter, a product of the turn-of-the-20th-century progressive movement that emerged in response to the corrupt politics that plagued cities like New York and Chicago.

Despite the radical and experimental origins of LA’s decentralized governance approach, a weak mayoral office may no longer be the best way to serve the people of Los Angeles today. Even if LA elected a progressive, Mamdani-esque candidate, the mayor’s office still has an uphill battle with fragmentation and decades of mounting red tape designed to favor negotiators over visionaries for mayor.

snippet.title: Sleep to History: The Day Money Died (Weimar Hyperinflation Documentary)
snippet.description:
Travel back in time to 1923 Weimar Germany, a surreal moment in history when money lost all meaning and a wheelbarrow of cash couldn't buy a loaf of bread. This relaxing history documentary explores the incredible story of the Weimar Hyperinflation—from the printing presses running day and night to the trillion-mark notes that littered the streets.

Designed as a sleep story, this video guides you gently through the economic chaos, the French occupation of the Ruhr, and the eventual stabilization of the currency, helping you unwind while learning about one of economics' most fascinating disasters. Whether you are looking to fall asleep or just want to learn history in a calm, low-stakes environment, let this story of inflation, resilience, and recovery carry you to rest.

In this video, you will learn about:
-The Treaty of Versailles and Germany's post-WWI economic struggles.
-How the printing of money spiraled into uncontrollable hyperinflation.
-The daily absurdity of life where prices doubled every few hours.
-The winners and losers of the economic collapse.
-How the Rentenmark finally stopped the chaos.

snippet.title: Obesity, diabetes and heart disease rates skyrocketing... is sugar to blame? (Full Documentary)
snippet.description:
How did the food industry get us to stop asking the question: is sugar toxic? It all starts with a secret PR campaign dating back to the 1970s. For forty years, Big Sugar deflected all threats to its multi-billion dollar empire, while sweetening the world’s food supply. As obesity, diabetes, and heart disease rates skyrocket, doctors are now treating the first generation of children suffering from fatty liver disease. The sugar industry is once again under siege. They dodged the bullet once. Will they do it again?

-------

-------

Today, industry is deploying its old tactics and pulling out the old adage “we just eat too damn much.”  This time consumers aren’t buying it. The critics have gotten smarter, bolder, and madder and science is catching up. 
  
Pediatric endocrinologist, Dr. Robert Lustig thinks we’ve all been ‘frucked’ by industry. He’s evangelical, blaming sugar for a waiting room filled with obese kids with fatty livers. His flock of five million online followers grows daily. In the court of public opinion, he’s part of a leading group of experts who are putting sugar on trial. 
  
But Japan’s not waiting for the verdict. For the first time in history, their children are burdened with 
lifestyle diseases that their parents never faced. To counter a health crisis that could sink their economy, Japan’s introduced a radical new law that takes aim at another 'bottom line': the girth of the nation's waistlines.  
 
Pulling back the curtain on the sugar-coated tactics of an industry once again under attack, Sugar 
Coated provides a chilling feeling of déjà vu. Today the industry is back sweetening the message. But this time, history comes knocking.  
 
When the doors closed at the Great Western Sugar Company in Colorado in 1976, someone forgot to sweep the floor. Gathering dust in the archives were 1500 pages of internal documents exposing how the sugar industry used tobacco-style tactics to dismiss troubling health claims against their products. Denver dentist turned postdoctoral scholar at the UCSF School of Medicine, Cristin Kearns, knew she’d stumbled on something big: the industry’s secret playbook. Her mentor, Stan Glantz, the superstar professor from San Francisco who brought down Big Tobacco warns, it’s going to get dirty. 
 
While industry and science duke it out, are we sitting on a dietary time bomb?

snippet.title: How The Rich Survive People Hyperinflation (And How You Can Too)
snippet.description:
How The Rich Survive Hyperinflation (And How You Can Too)

What happens to your money when a currency collapses?

In 1923 Germany, people who saved their entire lives suddenly couldn't buy a loaf of bread. Bank accounts became worthless almost overnight. But strangely, some people became even richer during the same crisis.

This video explains the real mechanism behind hyperinflation.

From Weimar Germany to Zimbabwe, Venezuela, and Argentina, history shows the same pattern repeating again and again. While savers lose everything, those who understand the system often protect and even grow their wealth.

In this video you will learn:

• Why currency is not the same as wealth
• How the rich protect their money during hyperinflation
• The five strategies wealthy families have used for centuries
• Why debt can become an advantage during currency collapse
• What historical hyperinflations teach us about money and assets

This is not financial advice. This video is based on historical events and economic patterns observed across multiple hyperinflationary crises.

Understanding the system may help you see risks before most people notice them.

How Much Does It Cost to Keep One Soldier in Combat for a Year? | USA vs Russia vs China

What does modern warfare really cost?

Not tanks.
Not jets.
Not missiles.

Just one soldier—fed, paid, trained, equipped, moved, protected, and kept alive—for one year of active combat.

In this video, we break down the true annual cost per soldier for the world’s three most powerful militaries:

🇺🇸 United States – the most expensive fighting force in history
🇷🇺 Russia – mass manpower, lower wages, brutal efficiency
🇨🇳 China – centralized logistics, scale, and state control

You’ll see how costs explode far beyond salaries:
• Training & recruitment
• Weapons & ammunition
• Food, fuel, and transport
• Medical care & evacuation
• Intelligence, logistics, and command
• Veterans’ benefits and long-term costs

USA: $500,000 – $1,000,000+

Russia: $60,000 – $100,000

China: $120,000 – $180,000

Why does one American soldier cost 10× more than a Russian one?
Does higher spending actually mean better performance?

This isn’t just a military comparison.
It’s a story about how nations fight, bleed, and spend.

⚠️ War is not just fought on the battlefield—
It’s fought in budgets.

From salaries and training to weapons, logistics, fuel, food, intelligence, medical care, and advanced technology — every country fights war very differently.

Why does the U.S. spend so much more per soldier?

And how is China balancing scale, technology, and efficiency?

💥 The most expensive army isn’t always the largest — it’s the most complex.

snippet.title: The Day the Railroads Decided What Time It Was
snippet.description:
Right now, wherever you are in the world, you know what time it is. You glanced at your phone and did not think twice about it.

But the time on that clock was not decided by scientists. It was not decided by governments. It was decided, in large part, by American railroad companies in the 1880s — and then gradually imposed on the rest of the world over the following century, often over fierce objections.

The global time system that every person on earth now uses is not a natural feature of the world. It is a commercial solution to a logistical problem, dressed up as a scientific fact.

And some parts of the world are still fighting it.

snippet.title: US CHINA TRADE RELATIONSHIP
snippet.description:
As of April 2026, the US-China trade relationship enters a new and complex chapter.
Markets are reacting to a fragile truce balancing national security with economic necessity.
From Washington to Beijing, leaders are navigating a pragmatic shift in diplomatic relations.
High-level negotiations focus on de-risking, signaling a strategic cooling of previous tensions.
Central to these talks are reciprocal tariffs affecting critical high-tech sectors like semiconductors.
Global supply chains are being rerouted as nations seek resilience in an uncertain world.
Investors remain cautiously optimistic, with market data reflecting a momentary stabilization.
Despite underlying friction, the flow of goods across the Pacific continues at scale.
All eyes now turn to the high-stakes economic summit scheduled for late this month.
As policy shifts emerge, the world watches to see if this truce can truly endure.
